Applying for research positions: what each one asks for.

After a PhD, the same skills can lead to very different jobs. Each one reads your application with a different question in mind. Knowing that question before you write saves a lot of wasted effort.

Four positions, side by side

Postdoc

usually 1–3 years, in one lab

They ask
Can you push our project forward, fast?
Documents
CV, cover letter, 2–3 references, sometimes a short research plan.
Interview
A talk on your work, a conversation with the PI and the group.
Your edge
A close match to the lab’s methods or topic.

Assistant professor

faculty, building your own group

They ask
What will you build here over the next 5–10 years?
Documents
CV, cover letter, research statement, teaching statement, 3–5 references, selected papers.
Interview
Job talk, meetings with faculty and students, sometimes a teaching demo.
Your edge
A clear, fundable research vision that is yours.

Research scientist

industry research lab

They ask
Will your research matter for our products or problems?
Documents
CV or resume, sometimes a cover letter, publication list, portfolio.
Interview
Research talk, technical interviews, team fit.
Your edge
Strong publications plus evidence you can work with engineers.

Research engineer

industry or lab, building systems

They ask
Can you build and ship what research needs?
Documents
Resume, GitHub or project links, sometimes a short cover letter.
Interview
Coding or system-design interviews, a project deep-dive.
Your edge
Working code, real systems, open-source contributions.

The documents, in plain words

  • CV. Everything, in order. For academic roles it can be several pages; for industry, a focused one- or two-page resume often works better.
  • Cover letter. Why you, why here, why now. (I wrote a separate guide on cover letters.)
  • Research statement (faculty). Where your research is going, not only where it has been: two or three directions, why they matter, and how you will fund and staff them.
  • Teaching statement (faculty). How you teach, with concrete examples: a course you could teach, how you mentor students, how you check that people actually learn.
  • References. Ask early, give your referees your CV, the call and a short note on what you would like them to highlight. Remind them a week before the deadline.

A typical timeline

Faculty searches take the longest. Counting back from when you would like to start:

  • 12–9 months beforePrepare. Draft your research and teaching statements, update your CV and website, and ask your referees.
  • 9–6 months beforeApply. Most faculty calls close in this window. Tailor each cover letter.
  • 6–3 months beforeInterview. First-round calls, then campus visits with a job talk.
  • 3–0 months beforeDecide. Offers, negotiation, start date, visa and moving.

Postdoc and industry roles move faster, often a few weeks to two or three months from application to offer, and many are posted whenever funding or headcount appears. Keep your documents ready so you can apply within days.

Where to look

  • Japan: JREC-IN Portal, run by JST, lists most academic positions in Japan.
  • Europe: EURAXESS for research jobs across the EU.
  • Computing and HCI: the CRA job ads and the ACM Career Center.
  • Everywhere: mailing lists in your field, conference job boards, and simply writing to people whose work you admire. Many postdoc positions are never advertised.

One habit that helps: keep a simple table of every application: position, deadline, documents sent, referees asked, status. It turns a stressful season into a checklist.
